One of my favorite stories in the stem cell field is the debate about what are the different states of pluripotency.

Mouse and human embryonic stem cells have several morphological and expression features that separate them.

Mouse embryonic stem cells are argued to represent a more undifferentiated state of pluripotency when compared to human embryonic stem cells. So there have been several attempts to turn back time and attempt to reverse human embryonic stem cells to a state that is closer to what is observed in mouse embryonic stem cells.

In 2010 Hanna and Jaenisch published "Human embryonic stem cells with biological and epigenetic characteristics similar to those of mouse ESCs".

At the time this work was published it was known that conditions needed to culture mESCs and hESCs were quite different and not interchangeable. mESCs of even the less permissible strains could be maintained using LIF, that activates the the JAK/STAT pathways, and by inhibiting GSk3b and ERK for the stabilization of the core pluripotency network, while both mEpiSCs and hESCs are dependent on the media addition of bFGF/Activin.

One of the main points of this work came from the protocol they developed to culture naive stem cells. Hanna proposed that the key element to drive hESCs to the naive state was Forskolin, a small molecule shown later to function as a PKA agonist, that could actually contribute to silencing of Oct4 and Nanog.

At the time the paper was received with quite a bit of excitement despite some clear caveats, namely the fact that the naive cells were only so for a limited number of passages, and that the 3D bi-refringent look of the colonies was not exactly sufficient to coin these cells as naive. It didn't take long for suspicions that the cells that were being observed were actually [more alike to neural stem cells](Human and mouse induced pluripotent stem cells are deferentially reprogrammed in response to kinase inhibitors.)

The 2i media combination is a favorite in a lot of stem labs to maintain cells in naive conditions and forskolin seems to have quite mixed results. In a follow up work the authors proposed improved methods to generate these naive stem cells and demonstrated that under defined media culture these human cells could even contribute to the formation of chimeric mouse embryos when integrated into the morula.

Analysis and review of the data made available in this follow up paper seems to suggest that the controversy with the naive state is yet to come to an end. From pubpeer:

"Dear Dr. Hanna and Colleagues

I appreciate Dr. Hanna's response to this important discussion. This will facilitate the investigation of naive stem cell induction. I am not sure whether it is good way or not to show my preliminary result here, but want to show one data using newly-uploaded Gafni's RRBS data, because this discussion becomes one of hot topics in PubPeer and the induction of naive stem cells is one of the most important goals in this field.

http://s8.postimg.org/l7085pg5x/Cp_G_naive_primed.png

I downloaded BS/RRBS-seq data from three independent groups (Gafni et al. 2013, Takashima et al. 2014 and Guo et al. 2014), and compared methylation profiles of each naive ESC with those of pre- and post-implantatio embryo. I note that I am not a member of these three groups, and there is no advantage to blame specific group.

The uploaded figure shows the clustering and methylation profiles of 15,994 CpG islands, which are covered by all datasets. Gafni's naive ESCs are grouped with Takashima's primed ESCs and postimplantation embryos. In contrast, Takashima's naive ESCs are grouped with preimplantation embryos including ICM. As discussed here, this results supports that Takashima's naive ESCs are closer to naive state than Gafni's. Interestingly, the methylation profiles of Takashima's naive ESCs are also distinguishable from those of preimplantation embryos. The heatmap indicates that Takashima's naive ESCs are more methylated than ICMs. I think that Takashima et al. improved naive induction method much than previously-reported methods, but is not completed yet.

I am acceptable for any claims and comments to this result."

Have thoughts or anything to add to this story?

Lit Review- A story of pluripotency and naive stem cells

Naïve human pluripotent stem cells are definitely a hot topic right now. Last mont there were a lot of presentations and posters in ISSCR about about the topic, and I would expect to see a lot of papers in the future describing derivation and characterization of different kinds of naïve-like human PSCs. It is an interesting question in general how this kind of naïve pluripotency, or pluripotency at all, is maintained, since the state is practically a cell culture artefact. The cells in an embryo that are used to derive PSCs are normally only in a transient unstable state of pluripotency and are supposed to continue differentiation into other cell types. In a 2011 Cell Stem Cell Review Loh and Lim described pluripotency as a precarious ballanced state between opposing lineage specifying factors. This interpretation, as least in my mind, makes sense in the developmental context of the embryonic cells. The pluripotency factors could be seen as factors which prime the cell to be able to differentiate into different cell types in a response to different signaling cues. Thus the pluripotency factors would mainly work to poise the differentiation associated genes for activation. Based on this one could speculate that inhibiting the signaling factors which normally control the differentiation of the embryonic pluripotent cells, i.e. epibalst or ICM cells, one sholud be able to block the differentiation process and potentially maintain the cells in a pluripotent state.

There has been a number of different papers so far published for the maintenence of human naïve state PSCs and most of them use a bit different combinations of factors to maintain the state. The most commonly used signaling factors in all of the papers are 2i+LIF. LIF is used normally in the maintenance of mouse PSCs, but human cells can not be cultured using LIF although the LIF signaling pathway is expressed and activatable in human PCSs. This could let us speculate that the disconnect in the LIF signaling could be in the targeting of the dowstream factor STAT3 to the pluripotency genes. Curiously, a paper describing the conversion of mouse EpiSCs to mouse ESCs using KLF2, 4 or 5 and PRDM14 also has suplementary data showing the colocalization of these factors with STAT3 in the pluripotency factor loci. KLF2 and 4 have also been used in converting human primed PSCs to a naïve state 1, 2, therefore it could be that the KLF factors are important for reseting the LIF responsiveness of human PSCs.

The second factor in the mix is the GSK3b inhibitor CHIR99021 which functions as a canonical Wnt signaling activator. Austin Smith's lab has demonstarted in mouse cells that the GSK3b inhibition should alleviate the repression of the pluripotency genes by TCF3. The Wnt signaling activation could therefore directly promote pluripotency gene expression. However, the Wnt signaling levels may also have a ballance point at which the signaling promotes pluripotency versus priming the differentiation of the cells. It was also one of the inihbitors that needed to be titrated for it to work in their human naïve cell maintenance medium 2. In primed state Wnt signaling contributes to the priming of endodermal differentiation associated gene activation by promoting the cohesin complex formation at their promoters 3. The whole Wnt signaling part in PSC maintanance is a bit of a wild card still as WNT agonists with DYRK inhibition have been used to maintain human PSCs and I have also heard that some Wnt inhibitors (like IWP-2 or XAV939) could also help in maintaining human naïve cells... Who knows.

The third factor normally used in naïve cell culture is the MEK inhibitor PD0325901. This is inhibiting the MEK mediated ERK activation by phosphorylation and thus the MAPK pathway. Additional factors affecting the MAPK pathway were recently found by Theunissen et al. by screening inhibitors for their potential to maintain human cells in naïve sate. These molecules targeted the BRAF and SRC proteins. Also inhibitiors of other MAP kinase pathways, i.e. p38 and JNK pathways, have been used in addition to MEK inhibition to maintain human naïve cells 4. As far as I know the mechanisms for pluripotency maintenence by MAPK inhibition are yet poorly known. My personal guess would be that ERK activity controls the Pol II phosphorylation of primed genes and thus it should contribute to the control of the swithching between Pol II pause and elongation. MAPK inhibition could then possibly be one of the factors that can directly inhibit the differentiation cues by external signaling.

Now the problem with human naïve state manitenance could be that the human cells normally need a certain level of MAPK siganling to promote the maintenance of pluripotency gene expression (I couldn't find the articel I wanted to link but I try to find it later). In mouse PSCs this is probably not the case as the active LIF signaling would directly target pluripotncy factors for activation, either by promoting additional Pol II recruitment or other ways of controlling its elongation. This effect might be similar by over-expression of the plurpotency factors, which is a commonly used method for converstiong human primed cells to naïve state, to have them enhance the expression of the endogenous pluripotency factors untill the pluripotency signalign entwork can be reset into an FGF independent and LIF dependent state. Other small molecular factors, like forskolin, might use similar but less specific way of generally boosting the pluripotency factor expression while the enodogenous signaling is not sufficient to maintain the state (forskolin increases the cAMP levels leading to CREB and CBP activation and increased histone acetylation and gene activation if targeted to proper genes). Moreover general increase in histone acetylation by inhibition of HDACs can maintain pluripotent cells of different species.'

edit: Some more about the aPKC inhibition.

aPKC inhibition has been previously shown to be able to maintain the pluripotent state of both mouse and rat PSCs. This inhibitor has also recently found its way into the small molecule mixtures aimed for the maintenance of human naïve state PSCs 4 2. It is not yet properly know what the function of the inhibitor would be, but aPKC is normally a cell polarity protein located at tthe apical surface of cells. Assuming the function of the inhibitors would be to block the siganling cues that are normally controling the differentiation of the cells, the inhibitior would probably block the cell polarization event which normally in an embryo would happen in the ICM to epiblast transition. This would also fit in with the model of the presumed in vitro counterparts of ICM and epiblast cells, ESCs and EpiSCs (or naïve and primed PSCs). I am not sure what the downstream factros controlling the ICM to epiblast transtion are in an embryo, but at a slightly earlier step, at the morula to ICM and trophoblast transition, cell polarity signals to the downstream target Cdx2 via TEAD4 and the hippo pathway. At the ICM to epiblast transition the target genes fo the hippo signaling factors would most likely have changed to epiblast specific factros and for factors that prime the cells for the consecutive differentiation steps. Considering that the hippo pathway in general tends to respond to things like cell mechanical forces on the cells, cell density and actinstress fiber formation, it would be my number one guess for the target pathway for the aPKC inhibitor. Curiously the hippo pathway has also been recently implicated in the maintenance of the pluripotent state of human cells in so called TSO complexes (TEAD, SMAD, OCT4). In this model the TEAD inhibits the activation of primed mesendodermal genes and prevents the cells from preliminary differentiation. Now if the naïve state cells need to have active hippo siganling, i.e. YAP and TEAD absent from the nucleus, and the primed state needs to have inactive hippo signaling, i.e. nuclear YAP and TEAD, coversion of the primed cell to a naïve state should not be easy as the same signaling which would maintain the cells in the naïve state would also control the differentiation of the primed stae cells towards mesendoderm. This is however mostly just speculation and we do not yet know for sure what is going on in the cells, and whether the naïve state really is indicative of a biologically relevant cell type or just an artefact.

I am not sure until today if the naive stem cells are a real thing or an artifact. For all due effects most of the hESC lines were derived from embryos that didn't cut it in terms of quality and they were originally from couples that had trouble conceiving anyway, it is hard to think that these are the standard for our knowledge of pluripotency in humans.

Regarding WNT proteins, Niwa has a really nice overview of their roles, I think that as secretory proteins they control a lot of the cell-cell communication in the stem cell colonies, who know how this would play out in the embryo, they seem to act in a dose dependent manner.

As for one of my pet peeves, the 2i inhibitors and particularly the GSK inhibitor. I think you are trylly forcing the ESCs into an alternate state by making some of the cell division check points mute (a little bit like the p53 kd in reprogramming). I tend to refuse to use them because they seriously mess the cell karyotypes after a few passages and make sequencing a trainwreck because the alignments make sometimes no sense. It is funny how this effect is only reported in rat but pretty much everyone is aware that it also messes other models, like in this case.

We had two projects in the lab that tried to use forskolin, one of them was in EGCs and led to nothing and the other one was in HESCs, also leading to nothing.

We have a paper coming out in the next few months that is able to achieve stable culture of naive HESCs but it was through messing about with the metaloproteinases, we will see.

Nowadays I am quite sceptical about the differnt inhibitor approaches for pluripotent stem cells before testing them myself first. I have tested many of the different inibitors that have been published for improving reprograming efficiency, but most of them have not worked too well. I have also tried inducing iPSC in different naïve cell cocktails, but in my experience all the colonies that survive and grow in those conditions have been expressing the reprogramming transgenes.

Do you have a working hypothesis for the factors that are affected by the metalloproteinases that could affect the naïve state maintenance?

Messing the metaloproteinases seems to affect Cell Cell contacts and change intracellular signal transduction.

On the first step the colonies change morphology, then they change expression to a closer resemblance to mescs.

Finally they seem pretty ok with single cell passage.

Not really, their expression data changes to be effectively mesc like and it is not just a morphological change.
